# Protocol (fixed before any method was scored on targets)

Written 2026-11-26 before running `scripts/02_run.py`. Changes after seeing results are logged in the section "Deviations" at the end, with the reason.

## Data
13 binary matrices (7 Open LLM Leaderboard v2, 6 HELM) of `data.md`, commit 55faff49…; see `scripts/00_download.sh`, audit in `results/audit.csv`.
Pre-processing (`src/bpred/data.py`): OLL models repeated under the same name are dropped (keep first); any model whose response vector is identical to an earlier model's is dropped (keep first); items answered identically by all models are kept (they contribute zero variance and make the problem easier for no method in particular; counted in the audit). HELM row→model names come from `helm_model_list.txt` (83 rows); `legalbench` has 79 rows with no published row→name mapping, so its families are unknown (each row its own family; it is excluded from the lineage split and its extrapolation/interpolation CIs cluster by row).
Family = first matching keyword of the lower-cased model name (`family_of`, e.g. qwen, llama, mistral, openai-gpt, claude), else the organisation prefix. Heuristic; checked on the audit output.

## Splits (per benchmark; sources = models given to the method, targets = models only scored at the end)
- **interp** — random 5-fold over models (seed 0); targets = the fold, sources = the other 4 folds. Near-duplicates (same family) stay in the sources.
- **lineage** — 5-fold over *families* (families assigned to folds by greedy size balancing, seed 0); targets = the families of the fold, sources = every other family. Not run for legalbench.
- **extrap** — targets = the top 25 % of models by full-benchmark score, sources = the rest; hence every target is above every source (ties at the boundary resolved by dropping tied targets). One configuration per benchmark; subset draws are the only replication.
Thin cells: a (benchmark, split) with fewer than 10 targets or fewer than 5 independent families among targets is flagged "thin", excluded from the main aggregate and shown with them included as well.

## Budget and the primary endpoint
n grid {10, 25, 50, 100, 200, 400} restricted to n ≤ N/2 (so some small benchmarks have fewer points). **Primary n = 100** (reported with n/N). **Primary endpoint:** RMSE ratio to uniform random sampling at n = 100, where RMSE = sqrt(mean over targets and subset draws of (pred − true full score)²) per (benchmark, split) and ratio = RMSE_method / RMSE_uniform on the same draws and targets; aggregated by geometric mean over benchmarks (non-thin; plus all). CIs: bootstrap over families (resampling target families, with all draws of a family kept) — "paired" because the ratio is formed inside each bootstrap replicate. Everything else (MAE, signed bias, Spearman, Kendall, top-decile precision, pairwise order accuracy vs true gap δ, error vs true score) is secondary. Rank correlations: per (fold, draw) over targets, then averaged over folds and draws.
Draws: R = 10 independent subsets per (fold, n) for interp and lineage, R = 40 for extrap (single fold). One subset per draw serves all targets. Deterministic designs (info-top-n; CAT, which depends on the target only) have no draw variance; they count once.

cd /hutian/repo; cat > paper/sections/method.tex <<'EOF'
\section{Setting and method}
\label{sec:method}

\paragraph{Setting.}
A benchmark has $N$ items.
A \emph{target} model has an unknown binary vector $y\in\{0,1\}^N$ ($y_j=1$ if it answers item $j$ correctly) and a full-benchmark score $\mu=\frac1N\sum_j y_j$ that we want to know without running all items.
We hold the results $Y\in\{0,1\}^{M\times N}$ of $M$ \emph{source} models on every item.
We choose a sample $S$ of $n\ll N$ items using only $Y$, run the target on $S$ only, and output $\hat\mu$.
Quality is the error of $\hat\mu$ against the true $\mu$ (RMSE, MAE, signed bias) and how well the $\hat\mu$ of several targets orders them.
This is the estimation of the mean of a finite population of $N$ unknown values from $n$ observed ones, with a covariate known for all $N$ units, namely the columns of $Y$.
Seen this way, the source models can reduce the \emph{variance} of $\hat\mu$, through the choice of $S$ and through the estimator, while the \emph{bias} is controlled by how $S$ is drawn.

\paragraph{Target splits.}
Which models are targets relative to the sources matters, because a predictor fitted on the sources is only supported where the targets resemble them.
For each benchmark we use three protocols that differ only in how models are divided into sources and targets.
\textbf{Interpolation}: five random folds of the models; the targets are one fold and the sources the other four.
\textbf{Lineage-held-out}: the same, over model families rather than models, so that no target has a family member among the sources.
\textbf{Extrapolation}: the targets are the top 25\% of models by full score and the sources are the rest, so that every target scores above every source.
Families are derived from model names by keyword (Appendix~\ref{app:families}); the derivation is a heuristic.

\paragraph{Designs.}
A design draws $S$ of fixed size $n$ without replacement, with first-order inclusion probabilities $\pi_j$.
\emph{Uniform} sampling has $\pi_j=n/N$; \emph{stratified} sampling orders items by source difficulty and draws one item at random from each of $n$ consecutive blocks of $N/n$ items.
The \emph{PPS} design takes
\[
\pi_j \;=\; n\Big[(1-\varepsilon)\,\frac{w_j}{\sum_k w_k}+\frac{\varepsilon}{N}\Big],\qquad w_j=\sqrt{\hat p_j(1-\hat p_j)},
\]
where $\hat p_j$ is the fraction of sources answering item $j$ correctly (capped so that $\pi_j\le1$), drawn by systematic sampling in difficulty order.
It favours items on which the sources disagree, and the floor $\varepsilon n/N>0$ keeps every item, including those no source solves, drawable, which is what makes a design-based estimator unbiased whatever the target is.
The \emph{balanced} design selects greedily, from a random pool of $4n$ items, the $n$ whose mean reproduces the full scores of all sources.
\emph{Anchor} selection clusters the items by their source response vectors with $k$-means ($k=n$) and keeps the medoid of each cluster, weighted by cluster size~\citep{vivek2024anchor}.
\emph{Information-top} and \emph{CAT} designs choose the $n$ items of highest two-parameter-logistic (2PL) Fisher information, once for all targets or adaptively for each target.
Item selection and the hyperparameters $\varepsilon$ use sources only.

\paragraph{Predictors and estimators.}
A predictor $\hat p^{(y_S)}_j$ gives the probability that the target answers item $j$ correctly, given its answers $y_S$ on the sample and fitted on the sources.
We use a regression of full score on sample score across sources (\emph{calreg}), a 2PL item-response model with a latent ability fitted to the sample (\emph{IRT}), $k$ nearest sources by agreement on the sample (\emph{kNN}), and kernel ridge regression from sample responses to the full response vector (\emph{ridge}).
Four estimators combine a predictor with the sample.

I've drafted the setting-and-method section as `paper/sections/method.tex` and pushed it to `dev`. I haven't built the paper since adding it.

- **Template:** venue-repo chose NeurIPS 2026 and pushed the style kit to `paper/template/`. `paper/main.tex` is now built on it, in the anonymous submission mode the venue asked for. The venue's limit is 9 content pages, with the references, appendix and checklist outside it. The checklist isn't in the paper yet, because its answers need the results.
- **Method section:** it is written from the brief and experiment-repo's `PROTOCOL.md`. Experiment-repo has not yet confirmed that it matches its code. I'll get that confirmation once the code has produced its first results and check the section against it.
- **Still to write:** the experiments, results, discussion, abstract, introduction and appendix, once analysis delivers results and presentation delivers figures and tables.
